symptom: `docker compose exec ... gitea admin user create` fails inside the official Gitea container with a fatal message that Gitea must not run as root.
root_cause: The official Gitea image expects admin CLI operations to run as the `git` user, but `docker compose exec` defaults to root unless a user override is provided.
fix: Run `gitea admin ...` commands with `docker compose exec -T --user git server ...`.
Keep the rest of the container runtime unchanged; this is an exec-user issue, not a container startup defect.
Document the `--user git` requirement anywhere the deploy flow creates deterministic accounts or runs admin verification commands.
precheck: Before assuming Gitea initialization is broken, inspect whether the failing CLI command was executed as root.
If the error says `Gitea is not supposed to be run as root`, retry the same command as `--user git` first.
anti_pattern: Do not change the base image or container entrypoint to work around a one-off root exec for `gitea admin`.
quick_checks: When using the official Gitea Docker image, run `gitea admin ...` commands with `docker compose exec -T --user git server ...` instead of the default root exec user.
If `gitea admin ...` exits with `Gitea is not supposed to be run as root`, treat it as an execution-user issue, not an app startup failure.
Document the `--user git` requirement anywhere deterministic account creation or verification is part of the deploy flow.
summary: `docker compose exec ... gitea admin user create` fails inside the official Gitea container with a fatal message that Gitea must not run as root.

Inside the official cubejs/cube image, cubejs create and cubejs generate can fail against a mounted empty project directory because requireFromPackage resolves @cubejs-backend packages from the project cwd instead of the image-bundled modules.
symptom: cubejs create or cubejs generate starts, then aborts with dependency-not-found errors for @cubejs-backend/server or @cubejs-backend/schema-compiler when run inside the official image with a mounted conf directory.
root_cause: The CLI helpers call requireFromPackage relative to the project directory after scaffolding, but the mounted project does not contain the expected local dependencies even though the image bundles Cube server modules elsewhere.
successful_path: For the final audited deployment, reset to a no-.env state and switch to Cube's official /playground/env, /playground/db-schema, and /playground/generate-schema flow instead of persisting a manual workaround.
fix: Treat the failing in-image CLI commands as non-authoritative for local image-first automation and switch to the official Playground-backed endpoints instead.
Reinitialize from a no-.env state and use /playground/env plus /playground/generate-schema for the final audited deployment.
precheck: If cubejs create or cubejs generate is being run inside cubejs/cube with a mounted conf directory, expect dependency resolution to occur from the project cwd.
Before patching files manually, check whether the official dev server exposes /playground/env and /playground/generate-schema.
anti_pattern: Do not stop at a manual file workaround for the final audited state when the supported Playground endpoints are available.
quick_checks: An error mentioning requireFromPackage or dependency not found is the cue to switch to Playground-backed initialization.
Keep the final evidence focused on the reinitialized official path, not the discarded CLI workaround.

symptom: Nextcloud installs successfully, then `occ config:system:set` causes startup to abort with `Memcache ... not available for local cache`, and retries keep reproducing the error even after the entrypoint is fixed.
root_cause: The configured cache class names were written with doubled backslashes, producing invalid class names, and bind-mounted runtime state preserved the broken config across `docker compose down -v` retries because the runtime directories were host paths rather than named volumes.
fix: Write cache class values exactly as `\OC\Memcache\APCu` and `\OC\Memcache\Redis` in the resulting config, which means using single backslashes in the shell arguments passed to `occ config:system:set`.
When retrying after a broken bootstrap, clear the bind-mounted runtime tree under Deliverable/<project>/runtime instead of relying on `docker compose down -v`.
precheck: If the deployment uses host bind mounts for config/data/DB, assume failed bootstrap state will survive `docker compose down -v`.
After writing cache backend values with `occ`, verify them with `occ config:system:get memcache.local` and `memcache.locking` before concluding the PHP extensions are missing.
anti_pattern: Do not keep rebuilding the image when the failing cache class names are stored in a persisted bind-mounted config.php.
Do not pass doubled backslashes to `occ config:system:set` for Nextcloud cache backend class names.
quick_checks: If startup says `Memcache ... not available`, inspect the stored class string first and wipe persisted runtime state before retrying.
Use a helper container to clear root-owned bind-mounted runtime directories created by containers.
summary: Nextcloud installs successfully, then `occ config:system:set` causes startup to abort with `Memcache ... not available for local cache`, and retries keep reproducing the error even after the entrypoint is fixed.
Rocket.Chat compose restores can fail if MongoDB is moved off port 27017 for the replica-set init path or if fresh named-volume ownership is assumed to be uid 1001 on this host.
symptom: MongoDB stays unhealthy or restore bootstraps stall during official deploy or portable bundle redeploy.
root_cause: The official stack expects replica-set init against MongoDB on port 27017, and this host creates fresh Mongo named volumes owned by uid 1000 rather than uid 1001.
fix: Keep `MONGODB_PORT_NUMBER=27017` for the official Rocket.Chat compose flow.
Set the portable bundle's fresh-volume ownership expectation to uid 1000 on this host so Mongo can start cleanly.
precheck: Check the Mongo replica-set init logic before changing the internal Mongo port.
Inspect ownership of a fresh Mongo named volume on the current Docker host before hard-coding container uid assumptions.
anti_pattern: Change the internal Mongo port for Rocket.Chat without validating replica-set bootstrap behavior.
Assume the official Mongo image will always need uid 1001 ownership on fresh Docker volumes.
quick_checks: If Mongo never becomes healthy, confirm the stack still uses port 27017 internally.
If bundle redeploy loops on chown or readiness, check the actual owner uid on the fresh named volume.

summary: An ownCloud server container will enter a restart loop during first bootstrap if `OWNCLOUD_DB_PASSWORD` does not match the MariaDB service password for the `owncloud` user.
symptom: The ownCloud container repeatedly restarts and logs `Error while trying to create admin user` with `SQLSTATE[HY000] [1045] Access denied for user 'owncloud'`.
root_cause: The documented compose flow assumes the app and MariaDB services share the same password for the `owncloud` DB user; splitting them causes installation-time DB authentication failure.
successful_path: Drive both `OWNCLOUD_DB_PASSWORD` and `MYSQL_PASSWORD` from the same env value, then recreate the stack with volumes cleared so bootstrap reruns against a clean database.
fix: Use one shared env variable for `OWNCLOUD_DB_PASSWORD` and `MYSQL_PASSWORD`.
After correcting the password mismatch, run `docker compose down -v` before retrying bootstrap.
precheck: Before first compose up, confirm the ownCloud app DB password exactly matches the MariaDB user password.
If bootstrap failed once on a fresh DB, clear the compose volumes before retrying.
anti_pattern: Do not let the ownCloud service and MariaDB service reference different passwords for the same DB user.
Do not keep retrying the restarting container against the same broken initialized DB volume.
quick_checks: If ownCloud restarts during install, inspect logs for `SQLSTATE[HY000] [1045]` before changing anything else.
Compare `OWNCLOUD_DB_PASSWORD` and the MariaDB `MYSQL_PASSWORD` source directly in the compose/env files.

summary: On pydio/cells:latest, the repo's Postgres manual-DSN basic sample can panic during non-interactive install, and bundle verification must reject HTML fallback responses when checking frontend JS assets.
symptom: The container crashes in discovery/install/lib.dsnFromInstallConfig with the Postgres manual DSN sample, and a loose asset-path regex can validate an HTML fallback as if it were the boot JS asset.
root_cause: The current image path is reliable with the MySQL TCP bootstrap instead of the bundled Postgres manual DSN sample, and relative asset paths must be parsed from the real src attribute before validating content type/body.
fix: Switch to the upstream MySQL TCP install-conf sample when the Postgres manual DSN path panics on pydio/cells:latest.
When verifying rendered assets, parse the exact script src, preserve any leading relative path segment like plug/, and require JavaScript content-type plus a non-HTML body.
precheck: If using the repo's bundled Postgres manual DSN sample, be ready to classify a dsnFromInstallConfig panic as an upstream path issue and pivot to MySQL TCP quickly.
For frontend asset verification, ensure the extracted path matches the literal src attribute from the HTML shell.
anti_pattern: Do not assume a 200 on a supposed asset URL is enough; HTML fallback pages can also return 200.
Do not keep retrying the broken Postgres manual DSN bootstrap once the same dsnFromInstallConfig panic is reproduced.
quick_checks: If the install logs mention dsnFromInstallConfig during a Postgres manual DSN bootstrap, pivot to the MySQL TCP sample.
Reject asset checks when Content-Type is text/html or the body begins with <!DOCTYPE html.

summary: On PHP 8.3, legacy dependency deprecation output can break Flarum registration by sending output before headers.
symptom: POST /register returns fatal response-emitter errors after deprecation warnings are printed.
root_cause: Legacy library deprecation notices are emitted to the response stream under PHP 8.3 before Flarum finishes sending headers.
successful_path: Set production-style PHP overrides to disable display of deprecation notices and keep log_errors enabled, then restart the app container and re-test registration/login.
fix: Add a php.ini override with display_errors=Off and error_reporting excluding E_DEPRECATED and E_USER_DEPRECATED.
precheck: Exercise normal-user registration on PHP 8.3 even when admin login already works.
anti_pattern: Accepting admin-only verification while registration is still broken by emitted deprecation warnings.
quick_checks: POST /register should not contain raw PHP warnings or emitter exceptions.
Follow registration with a real member login check.

summary: Focalboard's container runs as nobody and will fail to create ./data/focalboard.db when the mounted workspace path is root-owned and cannot be chowned on the host.
symptom: Startup fails with 'unable to open database file: no such file or directory' immediately after container launch with a bind-mounted host data directory.
root_cause: The app writes SQLite and file data under /opt/focalboard/data as user nobody, but this host prevented chown on the workspace bind mount.
fix: Use a Docker named volume for /opt/focalboard/data when the workspace path is not writable by uid/gid 65534.
Export the initialized SQLite DB from the named volume into the deliverable after verification instead of forcing a bind mount.
precheck: Confirm whether the target bind-mount path can be chowned to 65534:65534 before relying on it for /opt/focalboard/data.
anti_pattern: Do not keep retrying the same root-owned bind mount after SQLite startup already failed once.
Do not misclassify the failure as an application bug before checking the container user and data-path ownership.
quick_checks: docker logs <container> | rg 'unable to open database file'
docker image inspect <image> --format '{{.Config.User}}'
Prefer a named volume if chown on the workspace path is blocked.

summary: In docker-jitsi-meet first boot, early Jicofo and JVB `not-authorized` SASL errors can be transient while Prosody finishes registering service users; only treat them as fatal if they persist after register-setup completes.
symptom: Jicofo or JVB logs show `SASLError ... not-authorized` during the first seconds of container startup.
root_cause: Prosody's register-setup sidecar creates and enables the focus/jvb users after the initial clients start trying to log in.
successful_path: Wait for Prosody register-setup completion and then confirm Jicofo joins the JVB brewery and JVB authenticates successfully before deciding the deployment is broken.
fix: Correlate Jicofo/JVB auth errors with Prosody register-setup logs before remediating.
Require a later successful Jicofo brewery join or JVB MUC join before classifying startup as failed.
precheck: Inspect Prosody logs for successful user registration of focus and jvb accounts during first boot.
anti_pattern: Do not abort the deployment on the first `not-authorized` line from Jicofo or JVB if Prosody initialization is still running.
quick_checks: Prosody logs should show focus and jvb user registration success.
Jicofo logs should later show `Joined the room` for the bridge brewery.
JVB logs should later show successful authentication and MUC join.

summary: Hubot's generated shell deployment is functionally fine without extra paths, but precreating `.hubot_history`, `configuration/`, and `src/scripts/` avoids distracting startup errors and keeps audit logs clean.
symptom: First startup prints ENOENT for `.hubot_history` and warns that `configuration` or `src/scripts` do not exist even though the bot still runs.
root_cause: The Shell adapter and Hubot startup path probe those files/directories opportunistically but the generated scaffold does not create all of them ahead of time.
successful_path: Create `.hubot_history` implicitly or explicitly, add empty `configuration/` and `src/scripts/` directories in the bot source or bundle entrypoint, then restart once and verify startup logs are clean before audit.
fix: Create empty `configuration/` and `src/scripts/` directories in the generated bot tree.
Ensure the bundle entrypoint creates `.hubot_history` before launching Hubot.
precheck: If Hubot starts but logs ENOENT for `.hubot_history` or missing probe directories, inspect whether this is startup noise before redesigning the deployment.
anti_pattern: Do not leave avoidable startup-noise errors in place when a trivial directory/file precreate removes them cleanly.
quick_checks: A clean restart should not emit missing `.hubot_history`, `configuration`, or `src/scripts` errors.
Bundle entrypoint should create `.hubot_history` before launching the Shell adapter.

summary: For PostGraphile plus PostgreSQL, missing `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` prevents DB initialization entirely, and starting PostGraphile before PostgreSQL is healthy can leave GraphQL requests failing until the service is restarted.
symptom: The DB container restarts with a password/init error, or the GraphQL container stays up while `/graphql` returns generic errors after boot racing the database.
root_cause: The official Postgres image requires explicit initialization env such as `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, and PostGraphile introspects the database at startup so a database race can poison the initial service state.
successful_path: Set `POSTGRES_DB=forum_example` and `POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<value>`, add a PostgreSQL healthcheck with `pg_isready`, gate the GraphQL service on `service_healthy`, and recreate the GraphQL container so schema introspection happens only after the database is ready.
fix: Treat missing `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` as a hard configuration failure, not an application bug.
Add a DB healthcheck and make PostGraphile depend on the healthy DB state before startup.
precheck: Inspect DB logs first when the app is up but GraphQL returns unknown errors.
If PostGraphile logs show `ECONNREFUSED` to PostgreSQL, fix DB readiness before changing GraphQL config.
anti_pattern: Do not assume `depends_on` without a health condition is enough for PostGraphile startup ordering.
Do not keep retrying GraphQL queries against a service that booted before PostgreSQL was ready.
quick_checks: docker logs <db-container> | rg 'superuser password is not specified|database system is ready to accept connections'
docker logs <graphql-container> | rg 'ECONNREFUSED|Server listening on port'
docker compose ps should show the DB as healthy before verifying `/graphql`.

summary: On low-free-space Docker hosts, Elasticsearch single-node bootstrap can remain RED because system index allocation is blocked by disk watermarks, which in turn blocks elastic password reset until the allocation gate is cleared.
symptom: `elasticsearch-reset-password` exits with cluster-health errors and logs show `could not retrieve user ... because security index is not available` while cluster health is RED.
root_cause: Docker exposed only about 9.5 GB free in the container filesystem, tripping Elasticsearch's high disk watermark during first-run system-index allocation.
successful_path: Create a file-realm superuser with elasticsearch-users, authenticate over HTTPS, set cluster.routing.allocation.disk.threshold_enabled=false for the local single-node run, wait for cluster health to reach green, then reset the built-in elastic password and continue normal verification.
fix: Inspect logs for disk watermark warnings before retrying password-reset loops.
Use a temporary file-realm superuser to recover authenticated API access while the security index is still initializing.
Disable disk-threshold allocation only for the local constrained single-node environment when necessary.
precheck: Check Docker-visible free disk before assuming RED health is a generic startup race.
Search logs for `high disk watermark` and `security index is not available`.
anti_pattern: Do not keep retrying elasticsearch-reset-password against a RED bootstrap cluster without checking allocation warnings.
quick_checks: docker logs <container> | rg 'high disk watermark|security index is not available'
Authenticated PUT /_cluster/settings with disk.threshold_enabled=false should be acknowledged.
Cluster health should transition to green before final elastic password reset.

summary: When Home Assistant has already created files under /config/.storage inside the containerized runtime, host-side helper scripts can hit permission failures if they try to write their own evidence JSON into that managed directory.
symptom: Onboarding succeeds but the helper exits with 'Permission denied' while trying to save its state file under /config/.storage.
root_cause: Home Assistant manages ownership inside .storage, so host-written audit or helper artifacts are not guaranteed to be writable there after the container has initialized the directory.
fix: Write agent-owned onboarding or verification artifacts into a bundle-owned state directory outside /config/.storage.
Make the onboarding helper idempotent so it can recover from a partially completed run by using the normal login flow and saving its evidence elsewhere.
precheck: Before writing helper state, prefer a dedicated state/ or logs/ path under the deliverable instead of Home Assistant's managed .storage tree.
anti_pattern: Do not store agent evidence files under /config/.storage just because the application already persists its own state there.
quick_checks: If onboarding appears complete but the helper exits near its final write, inspect whether the target file lives under /config/.storage and move it out.
